chunks.section: MuPACE: Learning to Pace Muon for LoRA Fine-Tuning
chunks.text: Jan Kobiolka Affiliation: Department of Computer Science Affiliation: University of Technology Nuremberg Christian Frey & Josif Grabocka Affiliation: Nuremberg, Germany Affiliation: {jan.kobiolka, christian.frey,josif.grabocka}@utn.de

Learning rate schedules are typically fixed before training begins, yet when fine-tuning large language models with low-rank adapters (LoRA), the appropriate scale varies substantially with the model, task, and adapter configuration. Practitioners re-tune a schedule for every new problem, yet a tuned schedule still cannot react to the training dynamics it encounters. We instead amortize learning rate selection across LoRA fine-tuning problems. We leave the base optimizer, Muon, untouched, so that its normalized update fixes the direction, and meta-learn only the global step size. Our method MuPACE is a small recurrent policy, meta-trained across a distribution of fine-tuning runs, that conditions on the observed trajectory and emits bounded adjustments to an interpretable analytic schedule. On 64 fine-tuning problems, MuPACE outperforms standard fixed schedules at a strong shared default on 64–78% of problems and is on par with the same schedules with per-task tuned peaks. Meta-trained only on models with up to 16 layers, MuPACE transfers one-shot to unseen tasks on models as deep as 64 layers, such as Qwen3-32B and Qwen3.8-27B, where a single run remains competitive with swept schedules.

Modern deep learning optimizers increasingly decouple the update direction from its overall scale. Adaptive methods such as Adam ( Kingma and Ba, 2015 ) and AdamW ( Loshchilov and Hutter, 2019 ) rescale gradients coordinate-wise, while more recent matrix-aware optimizers such as Shampoo ( Gupta et al., 2018 ) , SOAP ( Vyas et al., 2025 ) , and Muon ( Jordan et al., 2024 ) exploit the structure of neural network parameters. Muon, in particular, constructs updates for matrix-valued parameters by orthogonalizing the momentum update and has shown promising performance in language-model pre-training ( Liu et al., 2025 ) and LoRA ( Hu et al., 2022 ) fine-tuning ( Qu et al., 2026 ) . The perspective of separating the update direction from the step size is also reflected in the norm-based view of steepest descent ( Bernstein and Newhouse, 2024 ) . At iteration t t , the optimizer forms an optimization signal s t s_{t} from the gradient g t = ∇ θ ℓ ​ ( θ t ) g_{t}=\nabla_{\theta}\ell(\theta_{t}) , such as the gradient itself or the momentum estimate. We denote by 𝒪 \mathcal{O} the optimizer-specific map from the optimization signal s t ∈ ℝ m × n s_{t}\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times n} of an m × n m\times n matrix to an update direction d t ∈ ℝ m × n d_{t}\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times n} of the same shape, with the update scaled by the learning rate η t ∈ ℝ + \eta_{t}\in\mathbb{R}^{+} , i.e.: d t = 𝒪 ⁡ ( s t ) , d t ∈ arg ⁡ max ‖ d t ‖ ≤ 1 ​ ⟨ s t , d t ⟩ , θ t + 1 = θ t − η t ​ d t . d_{t}=\mathcal{O}(s_{t}),\qquad d_{t}\in\arg\max_{\|d_{t}\|\leq 1}\langle s_{t},d_{t}\rangle,\qquad\theta_{t+1}=\theta_{t}-\eta_{t}d_{t}.

The norm determines the geometry of d t d_{t} , while the step size η t \eta_{t} sets its magnitude. For example, the Euclidean norm yields the normalized direction s t / ‖ s t ‖ 2 s_{t}/\|s_{t}\|_{2} , whereas the infinity norm yields the element-wise sign direction. For a matrix-valued signal s t = U t ​ Σ t ​ V t ⊤ s_{t}=U_{t}\Sigma_{t}V_{t}^{\top} , Muon uses the corresponding spectral-norm direction d t = U t ​ V t ⊤ d_{t}=U_{t}V_{t}^{\top} , approximated in practice with a small number of Newton–Schulz iterations ( Jordan et al., 2024 ) . For normalized optimizers, the learning rate therefore plays a particularly important role. Normalization can improve progress in challenging landscapes such as river valleys ( Shen et al., 2026 ) , but it also reduces the influence of gradient magnitude on the update size. A small residual gradient can still be mapped to a direction of approximately fixed norm, leaving η t \eta_{t} responsible for determining whether the optimizer makes useful progress or overshoots the local solution. Step-size selection is therefore an important and distinct control problem.

In practice, this control problem is often solved by committing to a learning rate schedule before training begins. Common choices such as cosine decay ( Loshchilov and Hutter, 2017 ) and warmup-stable-decay (WSD) ( Hu et al., 2024 ) set η t \eta_{t} primarily as a function of training progress, while their overall scale is selected through hyperparameter optimization. This is expensive because finding a good learning rate schedule can require several training runs, and the resulting setting does not transfer across fine-tuning problems, as the appropriate schedule varies with the downstream task, adapter parameterization, batch size, and optimization budget ( Biderman et al., 2024 ; Lee and Lee, 2026 ) . This lack of transfer makes fixed schedules especially costly, since tuning the peak learning rate for every new problem adds an extra search procedure, while the resulting schedule still cannot react to the optimization trajectory.

We therefore ask the following question: Can learning rate schedule selection instead be amortized across LoRA fine-tuning problems? We introduce MuPACE ( Mu on P olicy for A daptive C ontrol across LoRA Fine-tuning E pisodes), a learned, trajectory-conditioned learning rate scheduler for LoRA. LoRA fine-tuning is especially relevant because only a few large organizations train large language models from scratch, while most users adapt existing pretrained models ( Bommasani et al., 2021 ) . Unlike previous learned optimizers that meta-learn the update rule itself ( Metz et al., 2022b ; Moudgil et al., 2025 ) , we leave Muon unchanged and meta-learn only its global step-size schedule. A small recurrent policy observes the optimization trajectory and predicts bounded modifications to an analytic schedule family, explicitly separating changes in overall scale from changes in schedule shape. The scheduler is meta-trained across a distribution of fine-tuning episodes and then applied one-shot to new problems, producing an adaptive schedule within a single training run without hyperparameter search or downstream-specific tuning.

To assess the effectiveness of our approach, we evaluate whether a single meta-trained scheduler can replace per-task learning rate search across a broad range of fine-tuning settings, spanning pretrained models, downstream tasks, adapter configurations, batch sizes, and training horizons. On 64 problems, MuPACE outperforms strong fixed defaults on 64–78% of tasks and performs on par with schedules tuned separately for each problem, while requiring only a single trial. Moreover, despite being meta-trained only on models with up to 16 layers, MuPACE generalizes in a one-shot manner to large-scale models such as Qwen3-32B and Qwen3.8-27B (both with 64 layers) on unseen downstream tasks. It achieves competitive performance close to that of swept schedules while requiring only a single run. Our key contributions are: • We introduce MuPACE , a meta-learned, trajectory-conditioned learning rate scheduler for LoRA fine-tuning that adapts a bounded analytic schedule while leaving the base optimizer, Muon, unchanged, enabling one-shot application without target-task learning rate search. • We show that a single meta-trained scheduler generalizes across fine-tuning problems and model scales. On 64 problems, MuPACE outperforms strong fixed defaults and performs comparably to per-task tuned schedules, while transferring one-shot to Qwen3-32B and Qwen3.8-27B on unseen tasks, where it remains competitive with tuned learning rate schedules in a single run.

The maximal update parameterization ( μ \mu P) jointly defines width-dependent initialization, parameter multipliers, and per-layer learning rates, enabling near-optimal hyperparameters to transfer across width ( Yang et al., 2021 ) . Depth- μ \mu P extends this principle to residual networks with single-layer blocks ( Yang et al., 2024 ) . Transfer has been related to approximately width- and depth-independent Hessian sharpness under feature learning ( Noci et al., 2024 ) , though for Adam-trained Transformer language models, standard parameterization with suitable per-layer learning rates also transfers and can outperform μ \mu P when per-layer constants are tuned ( Everett et al., 2024 ) . A parallel line of work concerns the shape of the schedule rather than its scale. Cosine annealing ( Loshchilov and Hutter, 2017 ) remains common in LLM pretraining, alongside warmup-stable-decay (WSD) schedules that maintain a constant learning rate before a terminal cooldown ( Hu et al., 2024 ) . Additional approaches include linear decay to zero ( Bergsma et al., 2025 ) and schedule-free optimization ( Defazio et al., 2024 ) . However, frontier labs remain divided on the choice of learning rate schedule. Kimi K2 ( Team et al., 2025b ) uses WSD, DeepSeek V4 ( Xu et al., 2026 ) uses a warmup, long constant plateau, and terminal cosine cooldown, whereas GLM-4.5 ( Team et al., 2025a ) and Kimi K3 ( Team et al., 2026 ) report favoring cosine over WSD. Fixed-horizon theory similarly predicts power decay in easier regimes and a WSD-like schedule in harder ones ( Li et al., 2026 ) . Much of this work, however, concerns pretraining from random initialization over a known token budget, and does not establish that either the learning rate scale or the schedule shape transfers across LoRA

Learning rates can also be adapted during training using heuristic or learned rules, rather than prescribed by a fixed schedule in advance. For example, the heuristic ReduceLROnPlateau scheduler ( Krizhevsky et al., 2012 ) reduces the learning rate when a monitored metric stops improving. More flexible schedules can be learned by differentiating through the training trajectory ( Maclaurin et al., 2015 ) , while Hypergradient Descent adapts learning rates online using hypergradients ( Baydin et al., 2018 ) . Related approaches include Self-Tuning Networks for bilevel online hyperparameter optimization ( Mackay et al., 2019 ) , D-Adaptation for automatically estimating an appropriate learning rate scale ( Defazio and Mishchenko, 2023 ) , and MetaOptimize for adapting step sizes based on their longer-term effects on future losses ( Sharifnassab et al., 2025 ) . In contrast, we amortize learning rate adaptation across a distribution of fine-tuning problems. After meta-training, a frozen trajectory-conditioned policy adapts one-shot to new problems within a single fine-tuning run, without downstream specific hyperparameter search.

Learning-to-learn replaces hand-designed update rules with meta-learned ones ( Andrychowicz et al., 2016 ; Metz et al., 2022a ) . VeLO ( Metz et al., 2022b ) scales this methodology to a general-purpose optimizer using a hierarchical architecture in which a per-tensor LSTM hypernetwork generates the weights of a small per-parameter MLP update rule. It requires no per-task optimizer hyperparameter tuning but incurs roughly 4,000 TPU months of meta-training. Celo ( Moudgil et al., 2025 ) obtains strong out-of-distribution meta-generalization with only 24 GPU hours by combining task augmentation with a learned per-parameter MLP update rule and a learned global scheduler, meta-trained in two stages. Celo2 ( Moudgil et al., 2026 ) further separates update-rule learning from step-size selection. It meta-learns only the update rule, leaves the step size tunable, and defers learning a generally applicable scheduler to future work. Closest to our setting, L3RS specializes learned optimization to fine-tuning pretrained models and learns, for each layer, both an update magnitude and a mixture of directions supplied by base optimizers using temporal and optimization-statistic features ( Kristiansen et al., 2024 ) . Our approach instead focuses on a smaller part of the optimization process. We keep the update direction from a fixed base optimizer, Muon, and meta-learn only the global learning-rate schedule for low-rank fine-tuning.

We compare MuPACE against three fixed learning rate schedules, cosine ( Loshchilov and Hutter, 2017 ) , constant (warmup to a flat peak) and WSD ( Hu et al., 2024 ) , which we run at a default peak of 10 − 3 10^{-3} , matching MuPACE’s default schedule scale for λ 1 0 \lambda^{0}_{1} (H1 in Section 5 ) and with the peak tuned per task by validation loss (H2 in Section 5 ). In the out-of-distribution setting (H3 in Section 5 ) we add Hypergradient Descent ( Baydin et al., 2018 ) , which adapts the learning rate online from the dot product of consecutive gradients and, like MuPACE, needs no per-task sweep. We run it as published and with the depth- μ \mu P post-scaling of Equation 6 applied to its learning rate, so that it receives the same multiplier as our learned scheduler. Every method runs the same Muon update from the same adapter initialization, so only the learning rate over time differs.

We evaluate MuPACE on 64 64 configurations sampled from the meta-training distribution with scale augmentation disabled, each fixing the model, dataset, rank, scaling, batch size, and budget. All methods share the initialization and data order. The fixed schedules run either at their default peak learning rate of 10 − 3 10^{-3} , which is at or near the best fixed rate for all three families (H1), or at a peak selected per task from seven log-spaced values in [ 10 − 4 , 10 − 2 ] [10^{-4},10^{-2}] (H2). MuPACE uses a single run. We report test loss at the iteration with the lowest validation loss.

We transfer MuPACE one-shot to Qwen3-32B ( Yang et al., 2025 ) and Qwen3.8-27B ( Qwen Team, 2026 ) . Both have 64 64 layers and width 5120 5120 , against at most 16 16 layers and width 2048 2048 in the meta-training deck. Further, Qwen3.8-27B adds a hybrid Gated DeltaNet linear-attention architecture the policy never saw. Adapters use r = 8 r=8 , a = 16 a=16 and T = 200 T=200 steps on eight unseen datasets spanning instruction following, math, code, summarization, question answering and translation ( Section A.1 ). We report test loss at the iteration with the lowest validation loss. For fixed-schedule baselines, we additionally select the peak learning rate from five log-spaced values in [ 10 − 5 , 10 − 3 ] [10^{-5},10^{-3}] , while MuPACE and each Hypergradient Descent variant use a single run.

chunks.section: H1: Meta-learned schedulers can outperform standard default learning rate schedules on in-distribution fine-tuning problems.
chunks.text: By default, MuPACE learns a bounded correction to a cosine learning-rate schedule, where the base schedule is scaled to have a peak learning rate of 10 − 3 10^{-3} . H1 therefore tests the value of this learned correction against cosine, WSD, and constant schedules at that same fixed peak. Win rates are tested against 50% using two-sided exact paired sign tests ( Dixon and Mood, 1946 ) with Holm correction ( Holm, 1979 ) across the three baselines ( α = 0.05 \alpha=0.05 ). The learned scheduler achieves lower test loss on 78%, 66%, and 64% of draws against cosine, WSD, and constant, respectively, all significant after correction (Figure 2 ). Median improvements are 2–4% across the three comparisons. A further check against cosine at its best global scale ( 2.154 × 10 − 3 2.154\times 10^{-3} ) 2 2 2 39 of 64 draws, sign test p = 0.10. gives a smaller, non-significant win-rate advantage, while the learned scheduler retains a median reduction of about 4%. Overall, the learned correction provides gains beyond a strong fixed default by adapting the schedule to the task and to the observed training trajectory (Figure 5 ).

chunks.section: H2: Meta-learned schedulers can eliminate per-task learning rate search while retaining competitive performance on in-distribution fine-tuning problems.
chunks.text: We repeat the H1 comparison against the per-task tuned baselines, comparing their validation-based learning rate search with our learned scheduler, which requires no per-task sweep. Sign tests are applied as in H1. Figure 3 shows that the learned scheduler approaches the performance of per-task tuned schedules without the cost of a learning rate sweep. Our learned scheduler wins on 44 % 44\% , 45 % 45\% , and 38 % 38\% of draws against tuned cosine, WSD, and constant, with median relative differences of − 0.28 % -0.28\% , − 0.24 % -0.24\% , and − 0.90 % -0.90\% . None of these win rates differs significantly from 50 % 50\% . Per-task tuning matters here as the best peak varies by roughly a factor of five across the baselines. To quantify how much of that tuning the learned scheduler makes unnecessary, we take the draws where tuning lowers test loss by at least 0.5 % 0.5\% over the default and measure the fraction of that gain the learned scheduler achieves in one run, ( L default − L learned ) / ( L default − L tuned ) (L_{\mathrm{default}}-L_{\mathrm{learned}})/(L_{\mathrm{default}}-L_{\mathrm{tuned}}) . The median recovery is 80 % 80\% , 83 % 83\% and 78 % 78\% against cosine, WSD and constant (Figure 5 ). Figure 3: Learned scheduler versus validation-tuned baselines on 64 64 tasks. (a) Win rates and Holm-adjusted sign-test p p values. (b) Relative test-loss reduction versus each tuned baseline, where positive favors learned. Dots show tasks, diamonds medians, and bars interquartile ranges. Figure 4: Learning rate applied by the learned scheduler on 16 16 of the 64 64 in-distribution tasks. Figure 5: Median fraction of the per-task tuning gain recovered by the learned scheduler in one run, on the draws where tuning improves test loss by at least 0.5 % 0.5\% .

chunks.section: H3: Meta-learned schedulers can transfer one-shot to out-of-distribution fine-tuning problems, avoiding per-task learning rate search while retaining competitive performance.
chunks.text: Figure 6 evaluates MuPACE on models and datasets that were both unseen during policy training, comparing a single MuPACE run against fixed schedules with the peak tuned by a five-trial sweep on each dataset. The tuned baselines reach slightly lower test loss, with median relative differences of 1.13 % 1.13\% – 2.43 % 2.43\% on Qwen3-32B and 2.59 % 2.59\% – 3.02 % 3.02\% on Qwen3.8-27B, and MuPACE wins on 2 2 of 8 8 datasets per model. This gap is the price of one run versus five. Given only one trial, the fixed schedules perform worse than MuPACE by 14 % 14\% – 18 % 18\% on average and need two to three trials to reach the same performance (Appendix C ). Against Hypergradient Descent, the other sweep-free method, MuPACE achieves lower test loss on every dataset for both models, whether Hypergradient Descent is used with or without μ \mu P post-scaling. Figure 6: MuPACE versus validation-tuned baselines and Hypergradient Descent on (a) Qwen3-32B and (b) Qwen3.8-27B. Values show baseline minus MuPACE test loss (positive favors MuPACE).

We ablate MuPACE’s meta-training, schedule parameterization, shape normalization, and depth-dependent scaling to assess the contribution of each module to its performance. Effect of meta-training. We compare against the same scheduler architecture with no meta-training, fixing all output heads at zero so it follows the default cosine schedule from Figure 1 . Meta-training lowers median in-distribution test loss and improves performance on Qwen3-32B (Appendix D ). Analytic schedule parameterization. We ablate the analytic schedule family by replacing the five heads defining Equation 4 with a single head that predicts the learning rate directly. Direct prediction has similar typical in-distribution performance but a heavier tail of poor runs and no wins against the baselines in the OOD setting, suggesting that the analytic parameterization primarily improves robustness (Appendix E ). Shape normalization. We remove the shape normalization of Equation 5 , so the shape parameters can also change the schedule’s overall magnitude. This has no in-distribution effect, and on Qwen3-32B normalization is better on five of eight datasets, a possible but not significant transfer benefit (Appendix F ). Depth-scaled baseline (fixed) schedules. We apply the same depth-dependent scaling Equation 6 to each fixed-schedule baseline at (i) its default peak and (ii) its best peak from an in-distribution sweep. On both models, MuPACE achieves lower test loss in nearly all comparisons. These results suggest that MuPACE improves beyond transferring depth-scaled schedules, with in-distribution tuned peaks (Appendix G ).

Depth-dependent post-scaling. We meta-train a variant without depth-dependent post-scaling. In-distribution performance is similar, but scaling improves test loss on all eight Qwen3-32B datasets, suggesting a benefit for one-shot transfer to larger models (Appendix G.2 ).

We introduce MuPACE, a recurrent learning rate scheduler that adapts an interpretable analytic schedule to the observed optimization trajectory while leaving Muon’s update rule unchanged. Across 64 fine-tuning problems, it outperforms strong default schedules and recovers 78–83% of the benefit of per-task tuning in a single training run. Although meta-trained only on models with up to 16 layers, it transfers one-shot to 64-layer models and unseen tasks, where a single run remains competitive with swept schedules. These results suggest that amortizing learning-rate selection can remove per-task learning rate search while retaining competitive performance.

chunks.text: Figure 7 shows how baseline performance changes when we allow more learning-rate trials, while MuPACE uses only one. We compare MuPACE against its untrained counterpart, whose output head is fixed to zero, corresponding to its initialization before meta-learning. This variant therefore produces the default cosine schedule shown in Figure 1 , together with depth-dependent post-scaling. The comparison isolates the contribution of meta-training beyond the schedule initialization. On the 64 64 in-distribution draws, our meta-learned MuPACE wins on 44 44 and reduces median test loss by 1.61 % 1.61\% (two-sided exact sign test p = 0.0037 p=0.0037 ). On Qwen3-32B, it wins on 7 / 8 7/8 datasets, with a median reduction of 6.66 % 6.66\% (sign test p = 0.0703 p=0.0703 ). Figure 9 shows the comparisons. chunks.section: Appendix E Ablation: Direct Learning-Rate Head
chunks.text: In the following ablation, we replace the five schedule heads of Equation 4 with a single head that directly predicts a learning rate before depth- μ \mu P post-scaling. We extend its range downward (approximately [ 1.1 × 10 − 8 , 9.0 × 10 − 2 ] [1.1\times 10^{-8},\,9.0\times 10^{-2}] ) to accommodate the small learning rates produced by the normalized analytic schedule (especially λ 4 \lambda_{4} ). Everything else remains unchanged. At initialization, this head outputs a constant 10 − 3 10^{-3} before post-scaling, so it must learn how the rate changes over time, including warm-up. The policy is meta-trained for 9000 9000 outer iterations. Figure 10 shows example schedules after meta-training, demonstrating that warm-up emerges through learning rather than being set by the initialization. The direct head clearly outperforms default cosine and WSD, but not default constant, and performs worse than tuned constant (Figure 11 ). Its median performance is close to that of the analytic scheduler, with a difference of only 0.4 % 0.4\% that is not significant ( p = 0.38 p=0.38 ), although it performs worse on a few tasks. On Qwen3-32B, it trails all tuned baselines across the eight datasets but consistently outperforms Hypergradient Descent (Figure 12 ). Overall, the analytic parameterization appears to improve robustness more than typical performance. Figure 10: Learning rates applied by the direct LR head on 16 16 in-distribution tasks.
